blockMcqs.question: Why is reading `arr[i]` O(1) regardless of index?
options: The array caches the last accessed element
Its address is base + i × size, computed directly
Indices are stored in a hash map
The CPU scans until it reaches index i
blockMcqs.explanation: Equal-sized contiguous slots make any address a constant-time formula.

blockMcqs.question: Why do contiguous arrays often beat pointer structures in practice?
options: They use less total memory always
Adjacent elements share cache lines, avoiding misses
Their Big-O is strictly lower
Pointers cannot be indexed at all
blockMcqs.explanation: Sequential scans stay in the fast CPU cache; scattered nodes miss repeatedly.

blockMcqs.question: What would growing a dynamic array by +1 each time cost?
options: O(1) amortized append, same as doubling
O(log n) amortized append
O(n) amortized append, total work O(n²)
O(n log n) total work
blockMcqs.explanation: Every append copies; 1+2+…+n is quadratic, so a constant factor is essential.

blockMcqs.question: Inserting at the front of an n-element array costs:
options: O(1), it just writes one slot
O(log n) via binary placement
O(n), every element shifts right
O(n²), each shift triggers a copy
blockMcqs.explanation: All n existing elements slide one slot to open the gap.

blockMcqs.question: Why is `result += word` in a loop O(n²) in Python?
options: Strings are mutable and reallocate constantly
Each concat copies the whole growing string
The loop itself is quadratic
Hashing each word is expensive
blockMcqs.explanation: Immutable strings copy all accumulated chars per step; the copies sum to n²/2.

blockMcqs.question: With prefix array `P`, the sum of range [l, r] equals:
options: P[r] − P[l]
blockMcqs.explanation: P[r+1] is the total through r; subtracting P[l] removes everything before l.

blockMcqs.question: How do you rotate an array right by k in O(1) space?
options: Copy into a second array shifted by k
Reverse all, reverse first k, reverse the rest
Sort then slice at index k
Pop k from the end and push to front
blockMcqs.explanation: Three in-place reversals achieve the rotation without an extra array.

blockMcqs.question: Compared to an array, a linked list gives you:
options: O(1) random access by index
Better cache locality on scans
O(1) insert when you already hold the node
Lower memory per element
blockMcqs.explanation: Lists trade away O(1) indexing and locality for cheap insertion at a known node.

blockMcqs.question: Why must Go programmers write `s = append(s, x)`?
options: append mutates the slice header in place
A resize may move the backing array, returning a new header
Go slices are immutable like strings
It resets the slice length to zero otherwise
blockMcqs.explanation: Reallocation on growth gives a new backing array, so the returned header must be kept.

blockMcqs.question: Calling "append is slow because resizing is O(n)" is wrong because:
options: Resizing is actually O(log n)
Append is O(1) amortized across many calls
Arrays never resize in practice
Worst case and average are identical here
blockMcqs.explanation: Rare doublings spread their cost so the per-append average stays constant.
